(3)
Upper/Lower Limit Comparison for A/D Conversion Results
The ADCAn can check if A/D conversion results lie within a configurable value 
range.
This function can be enabled or disabled for each channel in ADCAnCTL2.
For the enabled channel, the A/D conversion result is compared with the 
specified lower limit (in ADCAnLL) and upper limit (in ADCAnUL).
Error flag
If the A/D conversion result of a specified channel is below the lower limit or 
above the upper limit, the corresponding error flag ADCAnSTR0.ADCAnRCE 
is set to 1.
ADCAnSTR0 indicates the error status of upper/lower limit comparison for the 
latest A/D conversion result for every channel. This register can be used to 
check which A/D conversion results are outside the specified range.
The value of the result check error flag ADCAnSTR0.ADCAnRCE is also 
reflected in ADCAnLCR.ADCAnLER0, ADCAnDBiCR.ADCAnDBiER0 and 
ADCAnCmCR.ADCAnCmER0.
Error
interrupt
The error interrupt INTADCAnTERR is generated if an A/D conversion result of 
a specified channel is outside the specified range.

(1)
Diagnosis of A/D Conversion Circuit
The ADCAn can diagnose operation of the A/D conversion circuit.
The A/D conversion circuit can be diagnosed during normal A/D conversion 
operation. The ADCAn additionally converts the reference voltage 
ADDIAGOUT after the A/D conversion of CG0. If the result of this diagnostic 
A/D conversion differs greatly from the expected value, the hardware may 
have had an error or malfunction.
The diagnostic A/D conversion is enabled by setting ADCAnCG0.ADCAnDIAG 
to 1.
Note
The diagnosis of A/D conversion circuit is available for CG0 only.
The diagnostic A/D conversion is started after the A/D conversion of the last 
channel of CG0 is completed.
• The A/D conversion results of CG0 are stored in the normal A/D conversion 
result register (see section 25.3.9 (1), A/D Conversion Result Registers).
• The diagnostic A/D conversion result is stored in ADCAnDGCR.
Diagnosis
procedure
1.
Power on the ADCAn by setting ADCAnCTL1.ADCAnGPS to 1.
2.
Set CG0 and the A/D conversion mode as follows:
– Set ADCAnCG0.ADCAnDIAG to 1 to enable the diagnostic A/D 
conversion of the reference voltage.
For example, write 8000 000EH to first convert the analog input voltages 
of CH1, CH2, and CH3, and then convert the reference voltage signal 
ADDIAGOUT for diagnosis.
– Set ADCAnIOC0.ADCAnCG0IDG to 1 to generate the A/D conversion 
end interrupt INTADCAnT0 at the end of the diagnostic A/D conversion.
3.
Specify the reference voltage signal ADDIAGOUT in 
ADCAnDGCTL0.ADCAnPSEL[2:0].
For example, set ADCAnDGCTL0.ADCAnPSEL[2:0] to 010B to use the 
reference voltage 1/2 AVDD.
4.
Enable the ADCAn by setting ADCAnCTL0.ADCAnCE to 1.
5.
Generate software or hardware start trigger to start the A/D conversion.
6.
When the A/D conversion end interrupt INTADCAnT0 occurs, read the A/D 
conversion results of the diagnostic A/D conversion in ADCAnDGCR.

INTADCAnT0 is generated.

Restrictions when Using Sample and Hold Function
Restrictions when using sample and hold function are as follows.
(1) The channels to which the channel sample and hold function is applied 
must not be assigned to multiple CGs at the same time.
Example 1: When the channel sample and hold function is applied to CG0, 
CG1, and CG2 (CG0 in one-shot conversion mode)
The following combination is possible.
– CG0 (CH1 selected), CG1 (CH2 selected), and CG2 (CH3 selected)
The following combinations are prohibited.
– CG0 (CH1 selected), CG1 (CH1 selected), and CG2 (CH2 and CH3 
selected)
Example 2: When the channel sample and hold function is applied to CG1 and 
CG2 (CG0 in continuous conversion mode)
The following combinations are possible.
– CG0 (CH1 selected), CG1 (CH1 and CH2 selected), and CG2 (CH3 
selected)
– CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH3 selected), CG1 (CH1 selected), and CG2 
(CH2 and CH3 selected)
The following combination is prohibited.
– CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH3 selected), CG1 (CH1 and CH2 selected), and 
CG2 (CH2 and CH3 selected)
(2) When changing the scan list of CGi to which the channel sample and hold 
function is applied during A/D conversion, set the scan list so that the 
channels for applying the function are not changed.
Example: When the channel sample and hold function is applied to CH1, CH2, 
and CH3.
The following changes are possible.
– Change from CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH3) to CG0 (CH1, CH2, CH3, 
CH10, and CH11)
– Change from CG0 (CH1, CH2, CH3, CH10, and CH11) to CG0 (CH1, 
CH2, and CH3)
– Change from CG0 (CH7, CH8, and CH9) to CG0 (CH10, CH11, and 
CH12)
The following changes are prohibited.
– Change from CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH3) to CG0 (CH1 and CH2)
– Change from CG0 (CH1) to CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH3)
– Change from CG0 (CH7, CH8, and CH9) to CG0 (CH1, CH7, CH8, and 
CH9)
– Change from CG0 (CH1, CH2, and CH9) to CG0 (CH9, CH10, and CH11)

25.3.15
Stabilization Control
The A/D converter needs time to stabilize operation at power on of the A/D 
converter (ADCAnCTL1.ADCAnGPS = 1).
Although a start trigger is acceptable even during the stabilization time, A/D 
conversion is not started before the stabilization time has elapsed.
In order to secure the minimum stabilization time, the setting of the stabilization 
time counter ADCAnCNT must be adapted (the counter should be set so that 
the stabilization time is not less than the Power-down return time (refer to 
Section 28 Electrical Characteristics)).

the conversion can be resumed later, and releases the hold state upon 
completion of the higher-priority A/D conversion).

completed, and starts the A/D conversion of the higher-priority CG (even if a 
higher-priority trigger is generated, the A/D conversion is suspended until 
conversion completion of the current channel; therefore the hold state of the 
trigger signal is released upon completion of sampling).

conversion of CGi is resumed.

ADCAnCGi – A/D Converter Channel Group Register i 
This register makes a scan list for each CG. Channels included in the scan list 
are converted in ascending order. For details, refer to section 25.3.3, Channel 
and Channel Group.
This register can also enable or disable the diagnostic A/D conversion which 
uses the reference voltage signal ADDIAGOUT, by using 
ADCAnCG0.ADCAnDIAG. For details, refer to section 25.3.11 (1), Diagnosis of 
A/D Conversion Circuit.
Access
This register can be read/written in 32-bit units.
Since this register uses master/slave configuration, the next A/D conversion 
channel can be set in the master register during current A/D conversion. The 
value in the master register is transferred to the slave register at the following 
timing:
• When CGi is not currently performing A/D conversion, the value is 
transferred 1 clock cycle (PCLK) after it is written in the master register.
• When CGi is currently performing A/D conversion, the value is transferred 
upon completion of the scan list conversion of the current CGi.
• If a stop trigger bit of CGi (ADCAnSPi bit) is set after the value is written to 
this register, the value is transferred when the A/D conversion is stopped.

25.5
Usage Notes
25.5.1
Range of Channel Input Voltage
Caution
The input voltage to the ADCAnIm pin should be within the specified voltage 
range. If the channel input voltage is above AVDD or below AVSS, the 
conversion result value of the channel is saturated and it may affect the electric 
characteristics of the other channels.
25.5.2
Stopping Conversion Operation
Writing 0 to ADCAnCTL0.ADCAnCE during conversion operation stops the 
operation and the conversion result is not stored in ADCAnCmCR.
25.5.3
Restrictions on Using Channel Sample and Hold Function
Refer to section 25.3.12 (2), Restrictions when Using Sample and Hold 
Function.
25.5.4
Application Design Notes
(1)
Analog Input Pin (ADCAnIm)
(a) The input voltage to the ADCAnIm pin should be within the specified 
voltage range. In order to avoid input of the voltage equal to or above 
AVREFnP or equal to or below AVREFnM, the input voltage is recommended 
to be clamped with a diode with a 0.3-V or less VF. If the voltage equal to or 
above AVREFnP or equal to or below AVREFnM is input, the conversion 
result value of the pertinent channel is undefined and cannot be 
guaranteed. In addition, it may affect the conversion result values of the 
other channels.
(b) Noise on the analog input pin (ADCAnIm) should be removed by 
connecting a resistor Re between the pertinent pin and the external analog 
signal input source and a capacitor Ce between the pertinent pin and the 
AVSSn pin.
(c) Crossing or close positioning of the analog and digital signal lines should 
be avoided as much as possible. The A/D conversion characteristics can 
be degraded due to noise induction or other possible causes.
(d) For both the input and output ports near the ADCAnIm pin, it is 
recommended to avoid high current drive and to use toggle switching as 
infrequently as possible.
(e) During self-diagnostic BIST, the voltage for the self-diagnostic circuit of 
ADCAn is generated from the voltage on the analog pin, so take care on 
this point when setting up the circuit (as a reference value, an impedance 
equivalent to about 56 kΩ is suitable when HEAPCLK is running at 80 
MHz).

(2)
Wiring of Power Supply
To minimize the influence on the A/D converter accuracy due to the factors 
such as switching noise on the digital circuit, the following measures are 
recommended.
(a) Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
(b) Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (EVDD, OSCVDD, FVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD (provided in 
some products only), VDDM, VDDC, AVDDn) and ground pins (EVSS, 
OSCVSS, FVSS, CPUPLLVSS, FRPLLVSS (provided in some products 
only), VSSM, VSSC, AVSSn). It is recommended to use approximately 0.1-F 
(reference value) multilayer ceramic capacitors or 4.7-μF (reference value) 
or greater tantalum electrolytic capacitors.
(c) We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDDn) from the digital 
power supply (EVDD, OSCVDD, FVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD (provided 
in some products only), VDDM, and VDDC) and supplying power via a 
series-connected regulator. When a common power supply is to be used, 
connect the analog power-supply line, digital power-supply line, and an 
electrolytic capacitor at a point in the source of the supply but wire the 
power supplies in isolation from each other on the board.
Insert a chip inductor at the point of entry for the analog power supply 
voltage. In addition, earth the analog ground, digital ground, and an 
electrolytic capacitor at a point in the source of the power supply, but wire 
them in isolation from each other on the board.
(3)
Analog Reference Voltage Input Pins (AVREFnP, AVREFnM)
Insert a bypass capacitor between the leads of the AVREFnP pin and the 
AVREFnM pin as close as possible to the leads. It is recommended to use 
approximately 0.1-F (reference value) multilayer ceramic capacitors or 4.7- 
F (reference value) or greater tantalum electrolytic capacitors.
(4)
Variation in A/D Conversion Results
A/D conversion results may vary according to the factors such as fluctuation of 
the power supply voltage and noise. Erroneous conversion results may also be 
produced if noise is generated on the analog input pin (ADCAnIm) and 
reference voltage input pins (AVREFnP, AVREFnM).
To prevent the system from being affected by such variation and erroneous 
conversion results, reduce them through software.
The following gives examples of using software to prevent bad influence.
• Perform A/D conversion multiple times and use the average value of the 
results.
• If A/D conversion is continuously performed multiple times and any singular 
conversion result is obtained, exclude it and use other results.
• If any obtained A/D conversion result is judged to be caused by a system 
error, do not handle the error immediately; first check to see that the 
erroneous result is caused again and then handle the error.

(5)
Hysteretic Characteristics of A/D Conversion
A successive-approximation A/D converter holds the analog input voltage in 
the internal common S/H capacitor and then performs A/D conversion. After 
A/D conversion is completed, the analog input voltage remains in the internal 
common S/H capacitor. This may cause the following phenomena:
(a) If the same channel is used for A/D conversion consecutively and the 
higher or lower voltage is used than the voltage having been used 
immediately before, the hysteretic characteristics may be presented, in 
which the conversion result is influenced by the value of the immediately 
preceding conversion, and the different conversion results may be 
obtained even for the same potentials. For reference, the hysteretic 
characteristics have a tendency to be great when the signal source 
impedance of the analog input pin in the external circuit and the resistor Re 
value are large, or the capacitor Ce value is small.
(b) If the analog input channels are switched to be used for A/D conversion, 
since a single A/D converter is used, the hysteretic characteristics may be 
presented, in which the conversion result is influenced by the value of the 
channel having been used immediately before and the different conversion 
results may be obtained even for the same potentials.
To obtain the more accurate conversion result, perform A/D conversion two 
consecutive times using the same channel and ignore the first conversion 
result.

25.6
How to Read A/D Converter Characteristics Table
This section describes the terms specific to the A/D converter.
(1)
Resolution
The minimum analog input voltage that can be detected, or the ratio of analog 
input voltage per one digital output, is called 1 LSB (least significant bit). The 
ratio of 1 LSB to full scale can be represented in units of %FSR (full scale 
range). %FSR is the range of the convertible analog input voltage represented 
in percentage. It is given by the following equation regardless of the resolution.
1 %FSR = (maximum convertible analog input voltage - minimum 
convertible analog input voltage)/100
= (AVREFP - AVREFM)/100
When the resolution is 10 bits, 1 LSB is expressed as follows:
1 LSB = 1/210
= 1/1024
= 0.098 %FSR
When the resolution is 12 bits, 1 LSB is expressed as follows:
1 LSB = 1/212
= 1/4096
= 0.024 %FSR
The conversion accuracy is determined by the overall error, independent of 
the resolution.

(2)
Overall Error
The overall error is the maximum difference between a measured value and a 
theoretical value.
It shows the sum of the zero-scale error, full-scale error, linearity error, and the 
error derived from the combination of these errors.
The quantization error is not included in the overall error in the characteristics 
table.

analog voltage to be sampled by the common sample and hold circuit.

conversion trigger to the start of A/D conversion.

Section 26 Peripheral Interconnection (PIC)
26.1
Features of Peripheral Interconnection
The peripheral interconnection (PIC) realizes various functions by 
synchronous operation using multiple timers and by connecting the timer 
internal signals between the timers.
Meaning of n
The unit number of each timer is represented by affix n (n = 0, 1).
For example, TAUAn represents TAUA0 or TAUA1.
Meaning of m
The channel number of the timer TAUA is represented by affix m (m = 00 to 15)
Meaning of x
Arbitrary value set for registers to be used
Meaning of y
The registers to be used are identified by affix y (y = 200, 201, 202, 203, 210, 
211, 212, 213, 30, 31, 50, 51).
Register addresses
Refer to section 26.3, Peripheral Interconnection Registers.
Clock supply
The PIC provides the following clock input. The PIC is connected to the PCLK.

Functional Overview

• Two-phase encoder function (control method 2)
• Three-phase pulse input control function
• Three-phase encoder function

 26.4.1.4
Example of Operation
(1)
Operation Example of Timer Configuration
In this example, an arbitrary combination of multiple timers (from among 
TAUAn, TAUJn, TSG2n, TPBAn, OSTMn, and ENCAn) that operate in 
arbitrary modes is started simultaneously.
(2)
Setting Procedure
1.
Initial Setting
Set the operating mode for each of the timers TAUAn, TAUJn, TSG2n, 
TPBAn, OSTMn, and ENCAn (register setting is included). (For details on 
initial setting of TAUAn, TAUJn, TSG2n, TPBAn, OSTMn, and ENCAn, see 
the section of each timer.)
2.
Enabling Simultaneous Start
Enable simultaneous start of the target timers by setting the corresponding 
bits in PIC0SSER0, PIC0SSER1, and PIC0SSER2 to 1.
3.
Start Trigger Output
Set the SYNCTRG bit in PIC0SST0 to 1 to start the timers selected in step 
2 simultaneously.
4.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 for the channels that are not yet started. This allows 
each of the different target timer groups to be started simultaneously in 
separate timing.

26.4.2
ADC Trigger Selection Function
 26.4.2.1
Functional Overview
The ADC consists of three channel groups and provides the ADC hardware 
triggers corresponding to each of the channel groups.
The internal trigger signals selected by ADCA0TSEL0 from TAUA0, TAUA1, 
ENCA0, ENCA1, TSG20, and TSG21 are ORed with the external trigger signal 
from the pin and the result can be input as the ADC hardware trigger signal for 
the pertinent channel group. Similarly, the internal trigger signals selected by 
ADCA0TSEL1 and ADCA0TSEL2 from TAUA0, TAUA1, ENCA0, ENCA1, 
TSG20, TSG21, TAPA0, and TAPA1 are ORed with the external trigger signal 
from the pin to generate the ADC hardware trigger signal for the pertinent 
channel groups.
The PIC provides the function to allow TAUAnINTm (internal trigger signal from 
each of TAUA0 and TAUA1 described above) to be selected as the ADC 
hardware trigger signal.
Caution
The trigger signals from the TAUA0 and TAUA1 channels are not controlled by 
the TAUAnMD0 bit in TAUAnCMORm. Accordingly, they are used as the ADC 
hardware trigger signals for all the interrupts.

Functional Overview
This function generates and outputs three-phase PWM waveforms with the 
dead time by using the set signal (timing signal for changing to active level)

The PWM output function of the TAUA sets only the clear timing in a period 
under the duty ratio specification. This function can set the set timing in 
addition to the clear timing to output more flexible PWM waveforms with the 
dead time.

 26.4.3.4
Example of Operation
This function generates and outputs three-phase PWM waveforms with the 
dead time by using the set signal and the clear signal generated once or less 
per one period.
• PWM output function
• One-phase PWM output function
The following function of the PIC is used to generate PWM waveforms 
supplied to the input TINm (m = 11, 13, and 15) of the one-phase PWM output 
function using the set signal and the clear signal generated by the PWM output 
function.
• RS flip-flop circuit
The three-phase PWM output function is actually implemented by assigning 
the one-phase PWM output with the dead time obtained by the above 
functions to the U, V, and W phases, which allows independent set/clear signal 
setting for the PWM output of each phase. Since the operation of the three 
phases is identical except for the channel assigned, only the operation of the U 
phase is explained below.
(1)
PWM Output Function
CH02, CH04, and CH05 are used in combination.
Setting the period, U phase set value, and U phase clear value to CDR02, 
CDR04, and CDR05, respectively generates the set and clear signals of the 
RS flip-flop circuit for generating the input TIN11 of the one-phase PWM output 
function using INT04 and INT05.
Similarly, for V phase and W phase, the set and clear signals can be generated 
using CH06 and CH07 (V phase) and CH08 and CH09 (W phase) instead of 
the above mentioned CH04 and CH05 for U phase.
(2)
One-Phase PWM Output Function
CH10 and CH11 are combined to allow the one-phase PWM to be output from 
TOUT10 and TOUT11.
By setting the dead time to CDR11, the one-phase PWM with the dead time 
inserted to the TIN11 input is output.

RS Flip-Flop Circuit
The RS flip-flop circuit receives the U phase set signal generated in CH04 and 
U phase clear signal generated in CH05 to generate PWM waveforms to be 
supplied to the input TIN11 of the one-phase PWM output function.
Figure 26-7
Operation Timing of RS Flip-Flop Circuit (Example of U Phase)
(1) When a signal is input to the input S, the output Q goes high at the rising 
edge of S.
(2) When a signal is input to the input R, the output Q goes low at the rising 
edge of R.
(3) The output Q is not affected by a signal input to the input S while the output 
Q is high.
(4) The output Q is not affected by a signal input to the input R while the output 
Q is low.
(5) When signals are input to the inputs S and R simultaneously, the input R 
takes precedence over the input S and the output Q goes low at the rising 
edge of R.
For V phase and W phase, INT06 and INT07 (V phase) and INT08 and INT09 
(W phase) are used as input to generate PWM waveforms supplied to TIN13 
(V phase) and TIN15 (W phase).
The PWM output function generates the timing to change the PWM output 
level generated by the one-phase PWM output function.
The PWM output function generates a set signal and a clear signal as the 
PWM active and inactive level output timing signals, respectively. The set and 
clear signals are input to the RS flip-flop circuit to generate the PWM signal 
that changes its level at an arbitrary timing.
The one-phase PWM output function generates positive or negative phase 
PWM and inserts the dead time according to the changes of the generated 
PWM signal, and then outputs the one-phase PWM signal.
The PIC provides a connection for using the set and clear signals generated by 
the PWM output function as the TIN input of the one-phase PWM output 
function through use of the RS flip-flop circuit.

The following describes the operation example of the timer configuration for V 
phase PWM output shown in Figure 26-10.
For the operation from the simultaneous timer start to PWM output by the one-
phase PWM output function, refer to the description of the operation example 
of the U phase.
(1) When CH07 (V phase clear signal output timing timer) for generating the V 
phase clear timing signal (INT07) is set to the value greater than the set 
value for CH02 (carrier period timer),
(2) CH02 underflow occurs before generation of the V phase clear timing 
signal (INT07) caused by CH07 underflow, allowing the set value for CH07 
to be reloaded.
(3) The above operation prevents generation of the V phase clear timing 
signal (INT07), which should be generated normally, and allows the V 
phase set timing signals (INT06) to be generated successively.
(4) In this case, PWM output waveform is not affected by the operation above 
because the V phase set timing signal (INT06) is ignored by the RS flip-
flop circuit. Accordingly, a waveform extending over two carrier periods is 
output as the PWM output.
(5) The PWM output changes at the next output timing of the V phase clear 
timing signal (INT07).

Section 26　Peripheral Interconnection (PIC)
 26.4.4.4
Example of Operation
This function is achieved by combining the following TAUA functions.
• Triangle wave PWM output function with dead time
• One-shot pulse output function
The following functions of the PIC are used to generate the variable dead time 
range pulses for positive and negative phases to be inserted in the variable 
dead time range.
• Combinational circuit (PFN001, PNF023, and PNF045)
In addition, the following functions of the PIC are used to synthesize the 
triangle wave PWM output waveform and the variable dead time range pulses 
to be inserted in the variable dead time range.
• Logical operation circuit (FN0i) (i = 0 to 5)
The high accuracy triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time is 
actually implemented by assigning the PWM output obtained by the above 
functions to the U, V, and W phases, which allows independent dead time 
setting to the PWM output of each phase. Since the operation of the three 
phases is identical except for the channel assigned, only the operation of the U 
phase is explained below.
(1)
Triangle Wave PWM Output Function with Dead Time
CH02, CH04, and CH05 are combined to allow the triangle wave PWM with 
the dead time to be output from TOUT04 and TOUT05.
(2)
One-Shot Pulse Output Function
CH10 and CH11 are combined to allow the pulse of the width set in CDR11 to 
be output as TOUT11 with a delay amount set in CDR10 behind the effective 
edge of TIN10 (TOUT02) of CH10.
This pulse (TOUT11) is used as the variable dead time range pulse that is 
used in the range where duty cycle is close to 100% or 0%.
Caution
Set each CDR for the one-shot pulse output function so that the following 
condition is satisfied.
CDR05  (CDR10 + CDR11)
If the condition above is not satisfied, the output waveform may be influenced. 
To minimize the influence, satisfy the condition above, and also fix the value of 
CDR11 to 0000H until the variable dead time range pulse is required.
Set the both edges to be detected of TIN10 (TOUT02) as effective, and set 
TAUAnTOL11 to 1 (active low).
Set the same operating clock for all the TAUAn channels that are used for the 
triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time and one-shot pulse 
output function.
For details on TAUA functions, refer to section 13, Timer Array Unit A (TAUA).

The logical operation circuit synthesizes the triangle wave PWM output 
(TOUT04 and TOUT05) from the triangle wave PWM output function with the

PIC0REG2n3k (k = 00 to 06).
Set the synthesizing logic for this function as shown in Table 26-21. The pins 
TAUAnO10 and TAUAnO11 output the signals synthesized according to the 
specified logic.
With the logical operations above, TAUA can perform the variable dead time 
control for securing accurate output when the duty cycle is close to 0% or 
100%, thus enabling output of triangle wave PWM more accurate than that 
provided by the triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time of the 
TAUA function.
The values to be set for V, VB, W, and WB phases are the same as those for U 
phase, although the channels and the register bits are different as shown in 
figure26-13 Block Diagram.
The PIC provides the connection for inserting the pulses generated by the one-
shot pulse output function into the PWM signal generated by the triangle wave 
PWM output function with the dead time through use of the combinational 
circuit and the logical operation circuit, which are provided as the PIC 
functions.

The following describes the operation example shown in Figure 26-16, where 
duty cycles of U-phase and UB-phase outputs change to 0% and 100%, 
respectively, using the timer configuration for U phase PWM output. The output 
of the triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time is active high.
(1) The triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time using CH02, 
CH04, and CH05 of TAUAn starts triggered by the start of timer operation.
(2) PWM waveforms with the dead time are output from TOUT04 and TOUT05 
by the triangle wave PWM output function with the dead time.
(3) A 0% duty cycle value is set in CDR04 for U phase output.
(4) The setting described in (3) sets the TOUT04 output to the inactive level 
and the TOUT05 output to the active level. Note that, however, the variable 
dead time range pulse is not output by this operation.
(5) To generate the variable dead time range pulse, a value for the variable 
dead time range pulse width is set in CDR11 when a 0% duty cycle value 
for U phase output is set in step (3).
In this example, the value of CDR11 is fixed to 0000H until the entry into 
the variable dead time range to minimize the influence on the output PWM.
(6) The variable dead time range pulse of the width set in CDR11 is output at 
the edge of TOUT02 after the elapse of the delay time set in CDR10.
(7) The pulse that is output in step (6) is converted to the variable dead time 
range pulse for U phase (FN00A) or UB phase (FN01A) by the 
combinational circuit PFN001.
(8) The pulses generated in step (7) are synthesized with the TOUT04 and 
TOUT05 output pulses in the logical operation circuits (FN00 and FN01) 
and are output from TAUAnO10 (U phase output) and TAUAnO11 (UB 
phase output).
(9) After step (8), variable dead time range pulse of a desired width can be 
inserted by changing the set values of CDR11, which specifies the variable 
dead time range pulse width.
Note 1. Since the variable dead time range pulses are sawtooth waves, they expand 
and contract on one side, unlike the triangle wave pulses, which expand and 
contract on both sides.
Note 2. Since one-side expansion and contraction applies to the variable dead time 
range pulses, a one-phase PWM output period in the variable dead time range 
is longer by half the width of an inserted variable dead time range pulse.

26.4.5
Delay Pulse Output Function with Dead Time
 26.4.5.1
Functional Overview
This function allows to generate three-phase PWM output with the dead time, 
that is, delayed as specified from the period timing.
With this function, PWM output can be reset in the next period unlike with the 
function described in section 26.4.3, Three-Phase PWM Output Function with 
Dead Time.

Section 26　Peripheral Interconnection (PIC)
 26.4.5.4
Example of Operation
The delay pulse output function with the dead time is achieved by combining 
the following TAUA functions:
• Delay pulse output function
• One-phase PWM output function
A PWM that is delayed from the period timing is generated using the delay 
pulse output function. Then the one-phase PWM is output with the dead time 
inserted using the one-phase PWM output function.
The delay pulse output function with the dead time is actually implemented by 
assigning the PWM output obtained by the above functions to the U, V, and W 
phases, which allows independent dead time setting to the PWM output of 
each phase. Since the operation of the three phases is identical except for the 
channel assigned, only the operation of the U phase is explained below.
(1)
Delay Pulse Output Function
CH02, CH04, and CH05 are combined to allow the base PWM for one-phase 
PWM output to be output from TOUT05, which has a delay amount generated 
using CH04 with respect to the period set using CH02.
CH03 is a reserved timer for function implementation; do not use it for any 
other function.
Caution
Do not set the delay amount larger than the period.
(2)
One-Phase PWM Output Function
CH10 and CH11 are combined to allow the one-phase PWM to be output from 
TOUT10 and TOUT11.
By setting the dead time to CDR11, the one-phase PWM with the dead time 
inserted in the TIN11 input is output.
Similarly, the one-phase PWM with the dead time can be output for the V and 
W phases using CH12 and CH13 (V phase), and CH14 and CH15 (W phase).
Caution
Set the same operating clock for all the TAUAn channels that are used for the 
delay pulse output function and one-phase PWM output function.
For details on TAUA functions, refer to section 13, Timer Array Unit A (TAUA).

PWM Output Using Three-Phase PWM Output Function with Dead Time 2
In the example shown in the above figure, the counter operation based on the 
longer clear time than period A is continued on period B using the three-phase 
PWM output function with the dead time to allow the PWM output A to be 
cleared at the beginning of period B.
Although PWM waveform A with respect to period A is the same as that 
obtained using the delay pulse output function with the dead time, the clear 
timing is used at the beginning of period B, thus preventing generation of the 
clear timing of PWM output B, which should be output in period B.
Moreover, the set timing of PWM waveform C with respect to period C is 
ignored because the PWM waveform is already in the set state. Therefore, the 
PWM waveform will not change until the clear timing in period C, resulting in 
the output of the PWM waveform that is synthesized from PWM waveforms B 
and C.
As described above, using the delay pulse output function with the dead time 
enables generation of more flexible PWM output timing than using the three-
phase PWM output function with the dead time.
The PIC provides the connection for using the PWM output timing generated 
by the delay pulse output function as the input of the one-phase PWM output 
function.

The following describes the delay pulse output example with the dead time 
shown in the Figure 26-27.
(1) Using the simultaneous timer start function, CH02 (carrier period timer) 
and CH04 (delay timing timer) are started.
Although CH05 (PWM duty timer) and CH11 (dead time timer) are started 
as well, they will not start counting until the INT04 edge and TIN11 edge 
are detected, where the former is the CH05 count start timing and the latter 
is the CH11 count start timing.
CH03 is not described here because it has no influence on the PWM 
output with this function.
(2) For CH04, CH02 underflow allows the set value in CDR04 to be reloaded 
to CNT04.
(3) CH04 underflow allows the delay timing signal (INT04) to be generated.
(4) INT04 generation allows the set value to be reloaded from CDR05 to 
CNT05, thus starting the count operation of CH05 (PWM duty timer).
(5) Here, INT05 is generated and the TOUT05 output level changes to the 
active level.
(6) Upon CH05 underflow, INT05 is generated again and the TOUT05 output 
level changes to the inactive level. TOUT05, which changes according to 
the CH04 and CH05 underflows like this, is supplied to the input TIN11 of 
the one-phase PWM output function.
(7) With the one-phase PWM output function, the PWM waveform with the 
dead time is generated and output according to the TIN11 edges detected.

 26.4.6.4
Example of Operation
The trigger and pulse width measurement function is achieved by combining 
the ENCAn interrupt trigger signals (ENCATnIEC, ENCATnEQ0, ENCATnEQ1) 
and TINn input pulse interval measurement function of TAUAn and TAUJ0.
Also, the DT circuit in the PIC is used to convert the interrupt trigger signal 
input to TINn into the level-sensitive toggle signal.
The trigger and pulse width measurement function implements measurement 
of the ENCAn output interrupt trigger signal interval using the TINn input pulse 
interval measurement function of TAUAn and TAUJ0.
(1)
TINn Input Pulse Interval Measurement Function
When the valid TINn edge of TAUAn or TAUJ0 is detected, the CNTn value is 
captured into CDRn and the CNTn is cleared.
Caution
Set the both edges (rising and falling edges) of TINn to be detected as valid for 
this function.
For details of the TAUAn and TAUJ0 functions, see the corresponding 
sections.
(2)
DT Circuit
The DT circuit is used to convert the interrupt trigger signal output from ENCAn 
into the level-sensitive toggle signal.
As shown in figure26-32 DT Circuit Operation, the output signal is toggled on 
each input interrupt trigger signal generation.
Figure 26-32
DT Circuit Operation
The PIC provides the input signal conversion and signal connection to TAUAn 
and TAUJ0 to measure the generation interval of interrupt trigger signals from 
ENCAn.

measurement function.

(1) Following signal is output from encoder timer ENCAn as a trigger:
- ENCATnIEC (interrupt trigger signal output when timer counter value is 
cleared by ENCAnEC input)
- ENCATnEQ0 (interrupt trigger signal output according to timing of a 
match of timer counter value and value of compare register 0)
- ENCATnEQ1 (interrupt trigger signal output according to timing of a 
match of timer counter value and value of compare register 1)
(2) The interrupt trigger signal output from ENCAn is converted to the level-
sensitive toggle signal by the DT circuit and is output to TINn of TAUAn 
and TAUJ0.
(3) By setting the both edges of TINn of TAUAn and TAUJ0 as valid, the CNTn 
value is captured into CDRn on the TINn toggle timing and cleared to 
0000H. This operation is repeated.
(4) When an overflow occurs, the count value FFFFH (FFFFFFFFH for TAUJ) 
is captured but the count value is not captured on the first trigger after the 
overflow.

 26.4.8.4
Example of Operation
By setting an arbitrary encoder count value to the compare value 
(ENCAnCCR1) of the ENCAn timer and enabling compare match interrupt 
(INTENCAnI1) of the ENCAn timer as the trigger of the pattern switch of timer 
TSG2n, the control of TSG2n output can be achieved.
In this control method, the encoder counter is cleared by a compare match of 
ENCAnCCR0 with the ENCAn timer value.
It is necessary to set compare value (ENCAnCCR1) at each pattern switch 
(each INTENCAnI1 interrupt). It is necessary to match the initial output pattern 
of timer TSG2n to the set value of the compare register (ENCAnCCR1) of the 
ENCAn timer before start because clear by Z phase input is not performed. 
Switching between normal and reverse rotations of output patterns should be 
set with the TSnPSC bit in TSnOPT0.

 26.4.9.4
Example of Operation
The encoder count value at which the TSG2n output pattern is switched and 
encoder count value which defines an offset of the output pattern switching 
position (advance or retard) are set in ENCAnCCR0 and ENCAnCCR1 of the 
ENCAn timer, respectively. Using compare match interrupt (INTENCAnI1) of 
the ENCAn timer as a trigger of the pattern switch of timer TSG2n, the control 
of TSG2n output can be achieved.
In control method 2, the encoder counter is cleared by a compare match of 
ENCAnCCR0. It is not necessary to set the compare value for each interrupt, 
unlike in control method 1.
The ENCAnCCR1 value can be rewritten with the INTENCAnI1 interrupt. It is 
necessary to match the initial output pattern of TSG2n to the set value of 
ENCAnCCR0 before start because clear by encoder clear input is not 
performed. Switching between normal and reverse rotations of output patterns 
should be set with the TSnPSC bit in TSnOPT0.

The timing of TSG2n pattern output is set in the TAUAnCDR5 and 
TAUAnCDR5 (m+1) registers of TAUAn.
The TAUAn capture values (TAUAnCDR4 and TAUAnCDR4 (m+1)) indicate 
the timing of rising and falling edges of the TSG2nPTSI2 to TSG2nPTSI0 pins. 
The variable phase control can be achieved by clearing and starting the timer 
TAUAn at the rising and falling edge of TSG2nPTSI2 to TSG2nPTSI0 pins and 
changing the TSG2n pattern output timing, in other words, changing the 
TAUAnCDR5 and TAUAnCDR5 (m+1) register values.

26.4.12
CAN Time Stamp Function
 26.4.12.1
Functional Overview
The time stamp function can be set for message reception by combining the 
CAN controller and CH1 or CH3 of TAUJ0.
CH1 or CH3 of TAUJ0 captures a timer value according to the TSOUT signal 
that is output from the CAN controller on reception of a data frame. The CPU 
reads the captured value and obtains the time when the capture event 
occurred, in other words, the time stamp of the message received via the CAN 
bus.

Section 27 On-chip Debugging Unit (OCD)
The on-chip debugging function is described in this section.
The on-chip debugging emulator allows the debugging of programs with the 
microcontroller mounted on the target system.
The debugging function incorporated in this microcontroller conforms to IEEE-
ISTO 5001TM-2003 Class 1, a Nexus debugging interface standard.
Caution
While the microcontroller supports the debugging functions described in this 
section, whether they are usable or not depends on the debugger. For details 
on debugging, see the user's manual for the debugger.
27.1
Functional Overview
An overview of the on-chip debugging function is given below.
(1)
Debugging Interface
This interface is used to communicate with the host via the on-chip debugging 
emulator by using the DCUTRST, DCUTCK, DCUTMS, DCUTDI, DCUTDO, 
and DCUTRDY signals.
(2)
Debugging Monitor
The basic debugging functions below can be used by running a monitor 
program in a memory space for debugging while the user-created program is 
suspended.
• Downloading of user-created programs
• Reading and writing memory and registers
• Running user-created programs starting at any address
(3)
Hardware Breaks
Up to four breakpoints can be specified for instructions and data. If a 
breakpoint is specified for an instruction, execution will be suspended at any 
address. If a breakpoint is specified for an address, execution will be 
suspended by access to data at any address.
Break conditions can be combined in sequences with up to two steps.
(4)
Software Breaks
Software breaks are used to suspend (cause a break in) the execution of user-
created programs stored in RAM at any address.
(5)
Forced Breaks
A user-created program can be forcibly suspended.
R01UH0098EJ0100 Rev.1.00

Section 27　On-chip Debugging Unit (OCD)
(6)
Forced Resetting
The microcontroller can be forcibly reset.
(7)
Real-Time RAM Monitoring (RRM)
Memory can be read while the program is running. Since this read access is 
through debugging-dedicated DMA, it barely affects program execution.
(8)
Dynamic Memory Modification (DMM)
Memory can be rewritten while the program is running. Since this rewrite 
access is through debugging-dedicated DMA, it barely affects program 
execution.
(9)
Measuring Times
Using a 32-bit counter, times taken to execute user-created programs can be 
measured based on a clock signal obtained by dividing the TCK signal 
frequency by two.
(10)
Masking
The following signal can be masked:
RESET
(11)
Selecting if Peripheral I/O Modules Run or Stop during Breaks
Whether peripheral I/O modules run or stop is selectable. 
• Peripheral I/O modules always stop operating during a break.
– Watchdog timer (WDTA0)
• Selecting whether modules run or stop during a break
– Timers (TSG2n, TAUAn, TAUJn, ENCAn, OSTMn)
– Asynchronous serial interfaces (UARTHn)
– Three-line serial interfaces (CSIGn, CSIHn)
– CAN controller (FCNn)
– A/D converter (ADCAn)
(12)
Hot Plug-in
The on-chip debugging emulator can be connected and debugging can start 
without resetting the CPU while it is running (hot plug-out is not supported).
(13)
Security
To prevent unauthorized parties reading the contents of the flash memory, a 
96-bit ID code can be written to the microcontroller. If the code the user inputs 
does not match the ID code written to the microcontroller when starting the 
debugger, the flash memory is not accessible. If the last bit (bit 95) is set to 0, 
the flash memory is not accessible even if the ID codes match.
For details of how to set the ID code, see the user's manual for the software 
tools you are using.
(14)
Trigger Events
The trigger events detect an event with four-step sequential execution on the 
execution address, the access address, the access data, and the range 
(comparison of large and small sizes).

27.3
Notes on On-Chip Debugging
1.
Handling of devices used for debugging
Do not mount a device that was used in debugging on a mass-produced 
product, because the rewriting of flash memory during debugging will 
mean that the number of times flash memory is rewritable cannot be 
guaranteed.
2.
If a pin reset is input while self-programming is in progress (the FLMD0 
signal is at the high level) in debugging mode (the DCUTRST pin is at the 
high level), debugging will be suspended. In that case, input the pin reset 
again while FLMD0 is at the low level.
3.
After placing the high level on DCUTRST, ensure that no resets are 
generated until ID authentication has been completed. If a reset is 
generated, it will cause self-diagnosis BIST to start, and this may cause a 
time-out and prevent communications with the tool.
4.
After power is supplied to the microcomputer, place the high level on the 
RESET pin while the DCUTRST pin is low. If the internal NEXUS function 
has not been initialized yet so that the signal on the RESET pin changes 
from the low to the high level while the signal on the DCUTRST pin is still 
high, release from the reset state will not proceed because internal signals 
are undefined, and the CPU will not operate. 
5.
This product does not support hot plug-out, which would handle turning off 
the supply of power to the NEXUS tool (including disconnection of the 
connector) in debugging mode. If the chip is booted up in debugging mode, 
do not turn off the supply of power to the NEXUS tool (including 
disconnection of the connector) during operations.
6.
After the chip is released from the RESET state and the transition of the 
level on the DCUTRST pin from the high to the low level, wait until at least 
10 cycles of the clock signal on the DCUTCK pin are input while the 
DCUTMS pin is at the high level and the DCUTRST pin is at the low level 
before setting the DCUTRST pin to the high level.
7.
Once the DCUTRST pin is at the high level, keep it at the high level (i.e. do 
not change the level back from high to low once the DCUTRST pin is set to 
the high level).
8.
Terminating operation in on-chip debugging mode under any of the 
following conditions causes operation to become undefined. After 
terminating operations in the on-chip debugging mode, set the RESET pin 
and the DCUTRST pin to the low level so that the start-up sequence for 
Nexus is executed.
– Power supply off
– Low level on the DCUTRST pin
– ID codes do not match
– FLMD0 pin and RESET pin are set to the high and low levels, 
respectively
9.
When the pin reset signal goes to the active level in on-chip debugging 
mode, the ERROROUT pin is fixed to the low level (when the pin reset 
signal is active in single-chip mode, the ERROROUT pin will be in the high-
impedance state).
10. After release from the reset state in debugging mode (with resetting 
produced by RESET, WDTA0RES, CLMA0RES to CLMA2RES, LVIRES, 
SGARES, or DBRES), a self-diagnosis BIST is not executed, waiting for a 
time corresponding to that required to execute the self-diagnostic BIST. 
Then, the self-diagnosis BIST reset is generated so that the transition to 
the state of running the user-created program is possible.

Caution 1. 
Implement the following countermeasures to minimize any adverse effect on 
precision of the A/D converter from the switching noise of the digital circuit.
i. Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
ii. Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FVDD, or 
AVDD0) and ground pin (VSSM, VSSC, EVSS, OSCVSS, CPUPLLVSS, 
FVSS, or AVSS0), and between the analog reference voltage pins 
(AVREF0P or AVREF0M) and the analog ground pin (AVSS0).
iii. We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDD0) from the 
digital power supply (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, or 
FVDD) and supplying power via a series-connected regulator. When a 
common power supply is to be used, connect the analog power-supply 
line, digital power-supply line, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point in 
the source of the supply but wire the power supplies in isolation from 
each other on the board. Insert a chip inductor at the point of entry for the 
analog power supply voltage. In addition, earth the analog ground, digital 
ground, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point in the source of the power 
supply, but wire them in isolation from each other on the board.
Caution 2. 
Connect resistor Re and capacitor Ce to the analog input pins (ADCA0Im) 
externally to eliminate noise (m = 01 to 18).

Caution 1. 
Implement the following countermeasures to minimize any adverse effect on 
precision of the A/D converter from the switching noise of the digital circuit.
i. Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
ii. Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD, 
FVDD, or AVDD0) and ground pin (VSSM, VSSC, EVSS, OSCVSS, 
CPUPLLVSS, FRPLLVSS, FVSS, or AVSS0), and between the analog 
reference voltage pins (AVREF0P or AVREF0M) and the analog ground pin 
(AVSS0).
iii. We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDD0) from the 
digital power supply (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, 
FRPLLVDD, or FVDD) and supplying power via a series-connected 
regulator. When a common power supply is to be used, connect the 
analog power-supply line, digital power-supply line, and an electrolytic 
capacitor at a point in the source of the supply but wire the power 
supplies in isolation from each other on the board. Insert a chip inductor 
at the point of entry for the analog power supply voltage. In addition, earth 
the analog ground, digital ground, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point 
in the source of the power supply, but wire them in isolation from each 
other on the board.
Caution 2. 
Connect resistor Re and capacitor Ce to the analog input pins (ADCA0Im) 
externally to eliminate noise (m = 01 to 22).
Note
Full-scale range (%FSR) is the ratio, as a percentage, of the extremes of the 
range of analog input voltages that can be converted, and is expressed as 
follows regardless of the resolution.
1 %FSR = (Maximum value of convertible analog input voltage - Minimum 
value of convertible analog input voltage)/100
= (AVREF0P - 0)/100
= AVREF0P/100
1 LSB is as follows at a resolution of 10 bits:
1 LSB = 1/210
= 0.098%FSR

Caution 1. 
Implement the following countermeasures to minimize any adverse effect on 
precision of the A/D converter from the switching noise of the digital circuit.
i. Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
ii. Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD, 
FVDD, or AVDD0) and ground pin (VSSM, VSSC, EVSS, OSCVSS, 
CPUPLLVSS, FRPLLVSS, FVSS, or AVSS0), and between the analog 
reference voltage pins (AVREF0P or AVREF0M) and the analog ground pin 
(AVSS0).
iii. We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDD0) from the 
digital power supply (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, 
FRPLLVDD, or FVDD) and supplying power via a series-connected 
regulator. When a common power supply is to be used, connect the 
analog power-supply line, digital power-supply line, and an electrolytic 
capacitor at a point in the source of the supply but wire the power 
supplies in isolation from each other on the board. Insert a chip inductor 
at the point of entry for the analog power supply voltage. In addition, earth 
the analog ground, digital ground, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point 
in the source of the power supply, but wire them in isolation from each 
other on the board.
Caution 2. 
Connect resistor Re and capacitor Ce to the analog input pins (ADCA0Im) 
externally to eliminate noise (m = 01 to 22).
Note
Full-scale range (%FSR) is the ratio, as a percentage, of the extremes of the 
range of analog input voltages that can be converted, and is expressed as 
follows regardless of the resolution.
1 %FSR = (Maximum value of convertible analog input voltage - Minimum 
value of convertible analog input voltage)/100

Caution 1. 
Implement the following countermeasures to minimize any adverse effect on 
precision of the A/D converter from the switching noise of the digital circuit. 
i. Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
ii. Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD, 
FVDD, or AVDD0) and ground pin (VSSM, VSSC, EVSS, OSCVSS, 
CPUPLLVSS, FRPLLVSS, FVSS, or AVSS0), and between the analog 
reference voltage pins (AVREF0P, or AVREF0M) and the analog ground pin 
(AVSS0).
iii. We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDD0) from the 
digital power supply (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, 
FRPLLVDD, or FVDD) and supplying power via a series-connected 
regulator. When a common power supply is to be used, connect the 
analog power-supply line, digital power-supply line, and an electrolytic 
capacitor at a point in the source of the supply but wire the power 
supplies in isolation from each other on the board. Insert a chip inductor 
at the point of entry for the analog power supply voltage. In addition, earth 
the analog ground, digital ground, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point 
in the source of the power supply, but wire them in isolation from each 
other on the board.
Caution 2. 
Connect resistor Re and capacitor Ce to the analog input pins (ADCA0Im) 
externally to eliminate noise (m = 01 to 22).

Caution 1. 
Implement the following countermeasures to minimize any adverse effect on 
precision of the A/D converter from the switching noise of the digital circuit. 
i. Use one full side of the board for the power-supply wiring or connect the 
wiring in as large a grid pattern as possible.
ii. Insert a bypass capacitor in the vicinity of the pin lead between power 
supply pins (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, FRPLLVDD, 
FVDD, or AVDD0) and ground pin (VSSM, VSSC, EVSS, OSCVSS, 
CPUPLLVSS, FRPLLVSS, FVSS, or AVSS0), and between the analog 
reference voltage pins (AVREF0P, or AVREF0M) and the analog ground pin 
(AVSS0).
iii. We recommend isolating the analog power supply (AVDD0) from the 
digital power supply (VDDM, VDDC, EVDD, OSCVDD, CPUPLLVDD, 
FRPLLVDD, or FVDD) and supplying power via a series-connected 
regulator. When a common power supply is to be used, connect the 
analog power-supply line, digital power-supply line, and an electrolytic 
capacitor at a point in the source of the supply but wire the power 
supplies in isolation from each other on the board. Insert a chip inductor 
at the point of entry for the analog power supply voltage. In addition, earth 
the analog ground, digital ground, and an electrolytic capacitor at a point 
in the source of the power supply, but wire them in isolation from each 
other on the board.
Caution 2. 
Connect resistor Re and capacitor Ce to the analog input pins (ADCA0Im) 
externally to eliminate noise (m = 01 to 22).
Note
Full-scale range (%FSR) is the ratio, as a percentage, of the extremes of the 
range of analog input voltages that can be converted, and is expressed as 
follows regardless of the resolution.
1%FSR = (Maximum value of convertible analog input voltage - Minimum 
value of convertible analog input voltage)/100
= (AVREF0P - 0)/100
= AVREF0P/100
1 LSB is as follows at a resolution of 10 bits:
1 LSB = 1/210
= 0.098%FSR
